records.entry: 1. The idea In economics the counterfactual is rarely observed. We cannot see what an economy would have done under a different interest rate, energy price cap, or fiscal package. The established tools for approximating it, structural models, synthetic control, local projections, each carry well-known limitations, so major policy decisions are often evaluated on contested evidence. AIDA proposes to build an open counterfactual laboratory for economics, using AI as a scientific instrument that changes how economic evidence is produced. The network trains 15 doctoral candidates to develop three interlocking families of methods, and to release them as open code, open models, and open benchmarks for the discipline and the wider RAISE community. The design principle is validation-ordered development. Build and test the instruments where validation is fast, cheap and checkable, in digital-asset and energy markets, then transfer them, under an explicit validity theory, to the questions where the stakes are highest, monetary and fiscal policy with central-bank partners. Introduction and Motivation Traditional portfolio theory, based on mean-variance optimization, is poorly suited for stablecoin analysis because it focuses on return maximization rather than price stability. Since stablecoins are designed to maintain a fixed peg (typically $1.00), their success should be measured by peg adherence rather than returns. Key Insight: No stablecoin has achieved perfect peg maintenance. Therefore, analysis should focus on understanding, predicting, and optimizing around peg deviations rather than treating them as anomalies.

Peg Deviation Framework 2.1 Peg Deviation Definition For a stablecoin with price $P_t$ at time $t$ and target peg $\pi$ (typically $\pi = 1$), the peg deviation is: $$D_t = |P_t - \pi|$$ The relative peg deviation is: $$d_t = \frac{|P_t - \pi|}{\pi}$$ 2.2 Peg Break Detection A peg break occurs when the deviation exceeds a threshold $\delta$ for a minimum duration $\tau_{min}$: $$\text{Break}t = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{if } d_t > \delta \text{ and } \sum{i=0}^{\tau_{min}-1} \mathbf{1}{d{t-i} > \delta} = \tau_{min} \ 0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ where $\mathbf{1}$ is the indicator function. 2.3 Break Severity Classification For a break episode lasting from $t_1$ to $t_2$, we define: Duration: $\tau = t_2 - t_1 + 1$ Maximum Deviation: $D_{max} = \max_{t \in [t_1, t_2]} d_t$ Average Severity: $\bar{S} = \frac{1}{\tau} \sum_{t=t_1}^{t_2} d_t$ Recovery Time: $\tau_R$ = time to return within normal range after break ends

Stability Metrics 3.1 Rolling Stability Measures For a rolling window of length $w$, we compute: Peg Volatility: $$\sigma_P(t) = \sqrt{\frac{1}{w-1} \sum_{i=0}^{w-1} (d_{t-i} - \bar{d}_w)^2}$$ Peg Persistence (fraction of time within normal range): $$\text{Persistence}(t) = \frac{1}{w} \sum_{i=0}^{w-1} \mathbf{1}{d{t-i} \leq \delta_{normal}}$$ Directional Bias: $$\text{Bias}(t) = \frac{1}{w} \sum_{i=0}^{w-1} (P_{t-i} - \pi)$$ 3.2 Stability Score A composite stability score combining multiple metrics: $$\text{Stability}_t = w_1 \cdot (1 - \sigma_P(t)) + w_2 \cdot \text{Persistence}(t) + w_3 \cdot (1 - |\text{Bias}(t)|)$$ where $w_1 + w_2 + w_3 = 1$ are weights.

records.entry: 4. Contagion Analysis 4.1 Cross-Coin Break Correlation For stablecoins $i$ and $j$ with break indicator series $B^{(i)}_t$ and $B^{(j)}_t$, the contemporaneous contagion is: $$\rho_{i,j}(0) = \text{Corr}(B^{(i)}_t, B^{(j)}_t)$$ 4.2 Lead-Lag Contagion The lag-$k$ contagion measures whether breaks in coin $i$ predict breaks in coin $j$: $$\rho_{i,j}(k) = \text{Corr}(B^{(i)}t, B^{(j)}{t+k})$$ 4.3 Contagion Network The contagion network is represented by the adjacency matrix $\mathbf{C}$ where: $$C_{i,j} = \max_k |\rho_{i,j}(k)|$$ This captures the maximum predictive relationship between any two stablecoins across all lags.

records.entry: 5. Peg-Optimized Portfolio Theory 5.1 Peg Covariance Matrix Instead of return covariance, we use peg deviation covariance. Regime Detection 6.1 Variance-Based Regime Detection Using changepoint detection on rolling volatility series ${\sigma_t}$: $$\hat{T} = \arg\max_T \left[ \sum_{t=1}^T \log f(\sigma_t | \theta_1) + \sum_{t=T+1}^n \log f(\sigma_t | \theta_2) - P(\text{change}) \right]$$ where $f(\cdot|\theta)$ is the likelihood function and $P(\text{change})$ is a penalty term. 6.2 Hidden Markov Model Approach State evolution: $S_t | S_{t-1} \sim \text{Categorical}(\mathbf{P}{S{t-1}})$ Observation model: $d_t | S_t \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_{S_t}, \sigma^2_{S_t})$ Parameters estimated via EM algorithm.

records.entry: 7. Stress Testing Framework 7.1 Scenario Definition A stress scenario $\mathcal{S}$ is defined by: Shock magnitude: $\Delta_S$ Duration: $\tau_S$ Recovery pattern: ${r_k}_{k=1}^{\tau_R}$ 7.2 Stress Application For baseline price series ${P_t^0}$, the stressed series is: $$P_t^S = \begin{cases} P_t^0 + \Delta_S & t \in [t_0, t_0 + \tau_S] \ P_t^0 + r_{t-t_0-\tau_S} & t \in [t_0 + \tau_S + 1, t_0 + \tau_S + \tau_R] \ P_t^0 & \text{otherwise} \end{cases}$$ 7.3 Resilience Metrics Maximum Deviation Under Stress: $$D_{max}^S = \max_{t \in [t_0, t_0 + \tau_S + \tau_R]} |P_t^S - \pi|$$ Recovery Time: $$\tau_{recovery} = \min{k : |P_{t_0 + \tau_S + k}^S - \pi| < \epsilon}$$ Stress Impact Score: $$\text{SIS} = \frac{D_{max}^S \cdot \tau_{recovery}}{\tau_S}$$

records.entry: 9. Empirical Applications 9.1 Portfolio Performance Evaluation Traditional Sharpe ratio is inadequate. Instead, use: Peg Stability Ratio: $$PSR = \frac{|\mathbb{E}[R_p]|}{\text{Std}[d_t^{portfolio}]}$$ Maximum Peg Deviation: $$MPD = \max_t |P_t^{portfolio} - \pi|$$ Peg Persistence Score: $$PPS = \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^T \mathbf{1}{d_t^{portfolio} \leq \delta{normal}}$$ 9.2 Hypothesis Testing Null Hypothesis: Portfolio peg stability equals individual coin average $$H_0: \mathbb{E}[d_t^{portfolio}] = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{E}[d_t^{(i)}]$$ Use paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test depending on distribution properties.

records.entry: 10. Conclusion This framework provides a comprehensive approach to stablecoin analysis that prioritizes the fundamental purpose of these assets: maintaining price stability. By focusing on peg deviations rather than returns, we can better understand systemic risks, construct more appropriate portfolios, and develop early warning systems for stability issues. The methodology addresses several key limitations of traditional financial analysis when applied to stablecoins and provides practical tools for risk management in the stablecoin ecosystem. Note: All parameters should be calibrated based on specific use cases and market conditions. The framework is designed to be flexible and adaptable to different stablecoin mechanisms and market environments.
